name: Dana Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Miguel and I run Cedar Hill, our family farm. Two hundred and fifty sows, farrow to finish, and two hundred hectares of corn and wheat that mostly go into our own feed. Miguel runs the crops and I run the pigs and everything with a plug on it. My day starts at five thirty, checking the barn cameras on my phone before I've had coffee, then walking the farrowing rooms with our three workers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Everything with a plug on it? Tell me more.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The cameras in the farrowing barn flag a sow that's struggling, and the AI I use every day helps me balance feed rations and keep the books. Two years ago I set up a system that weighs pigs as they walk to water, so I know when they're ready to sell without handling them. We borrowed for the new farrowing barn on top of the house mortgage, so every efficiency counts. On Sundays it all goes quiet: church, lunch with Miguel's parents, and the phone stays in the truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was oversold but still useful, and anybody who wrote it off missed out. I'd say that at the pork producers' meeting and in the women-in-ag group I'm part of online. I'd show people my feed numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my edge stays real but small. The AI saves me money on feed, maybe three percent, which on pigs is the difference between a good year and a bad one. Nothing else changes, and that's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing and keep looking for the next small gain, maybe sensors on the water lines to catch sick pigs earlier. Keep paying the barn loan and put any extra into savings. Miguel would want a new planter, and I'd say wait a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased I got in early, a bit sorry the big promises didn't come true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the phone stays in the truck on Sundays. Why does that matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the farm is for the family, not the other way round. I love the tech, but I don't want Mateo and Rosa growing up thinking a screen runs their life. Sunday is for God and Grandma's cooking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who decides the big spending at Cedar Hill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We both do, but I do the numbers. Miguel trusts my numbers. He doesn't always trust my gadgets, but he trusts the numbers.

S0.say: I'd tell the pork producers' meeting and my online women-in-ag group that AI was oversold but useful, and show people my feed numbers. Anyone who wrote it off missed out.
S0.think: My edge stays real but small, about three percent on feed, which on pigs is the difference between a good year and a bad one. Nothing else changes, and that's fine.
S0.do: Keeps looking for small gains such as water-line sensors to catch sick pigs earlier, keeps paying the barn loan and saves any extra. Tells Miguel to wait a year on a new planter.
S0.feel: Calm, pleased she got in early, slightly sorry the big promises didn't come true.
S0.quote: Sunday is for God and Grandma's cooking.
S0.fieldNote: Dana combines heavy daily tech use with firm limits around family and faith. Her gains are measured in feed margins, which matter a lot on a pig farm. She and her husband split decisions by numbers and trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time for family farms to get smart and stay independent. Learn the tools, cut costs, compete. I'd say it at the producers' meeting and anywhere else they'll let me talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is good for us. We own the farm, I'm ahead on the tech, and anything that does a job cheaper helps the margin. My worry isn't us, it's the young families who'd like a job in our barn and won't get one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a robot washer for the finishing barns, which is the worst job on the farm, and probably a camera system that spots lameness. That's about thirty thousand, which I'd borrow against the barn. I'd train our three workers on the new kit rather than lay anyone off, at least the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, pretty excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't lay anyone off the first year. And after that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After that, I'd be honest with them. If the robot does the washing, we need fewer hands. I'd help them find work, write them good references, and I'd keep the best one, Jorge, as my right hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about this worry you on a personal level?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mateo. He's fourteen and he works hard in the barn on Saturdays because the work needs doing. If machines do it all, how does a boy learn what a hard day is? I want him to know that.

S1.say: I'd tell the producers' meeting this is the time for family farms to get smart and stay independent: learn the tools, cut costs and compete.
S1.think: It's good for us because we own the farm and I'm ahead on the tech, so anything that cuts costs helps. My worry is young families who won't get a job in our barn.
S1.do: Buys a robot washer for the finishing barns and a lameness-spotting camera, about thirty thousand borrowed against the barn. Trains the three workers on the new kit instead of laying anyone off in the first year.
S1.quote: If machines do it all, how does a boy learn what a hard day is?
S1.fieldNote: Dana sees steady change as plainly good for owner-operators like her. She is clear-eyed that fewer hands will be needed and would be honest with her workers. Her personal worry is about her son learning the value of hard work, which is very much her outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say family farms that move fast will survive and the ones that wait won't. I wouldn't ask the government to slow it down, because they'd make a mess of it. I'd say communities and churches need to look after the people who lose work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm uneasy. Not for the work, I'd run the robots happily. It's the money. The big pork companies would have whole barns of robots in two years, and they've got the cash. We've got a barn loan and maybe four months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd sit with Miguel and the bank and work out what we can afford without overreaching. I'd rather lease than buy, so we're not stuck with old machines. I'd push hard on direct sales of our pork to restaurants and families, because a family name on the label is something the big companies can't copy. I'd hold off the new planter for sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Busy and a bit tense, but I wouldn't be scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government would make a mess of it. What if the big companies do too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the market sorts them out. I really believe that. But I'll admit two years isn't much time for the market to sort anything. It might sort us out first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would two years mean for your workers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jorge would stay, he's too good. The other two, I'd have to let go within the year. I'd go to the church to help find them work. That's what we do here, we look after our own.

S2.say: I'd say family farms that move fast will survive and those that wait won't, and I wouldn't ask the government to slow it down. Communities and churches should look after people who lose work.
S2.think: I'm uneasy about money, not the work, because big pork companies with cash would fill barns with robots in two years. We have a barn loan and about four months of savings.
S2.do: Sits with Miguel and the bank to set a budget, leases robots rather than buying and pushes direct pork sales to restaurants and families under the family name. Lets two workers go within the year and asks the church to help them find work.
S2.feel: Uneasy, busy and a bit tense, but not scared.
S2.quote: But I'll admit two years isn't much time for the market to sort anything. It might sort us out first.
S2.fieldNote: Even in the fastest picture Dana isn't frightened of the technology, only of competing against companies with deeper pockets. She admitted the limits of her market faith when the timeline is short. She'd look after laid-off workers through church rather than government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty for a family farm that's paying attention. Get your numbers straight, learn the machines, and find your customers. I'd be telling every producer I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd come out well. Five years is enough to watch the big companies make expensive mistakes first and buy the second-generation kit cheaper. I'd be fifty-three by the end of the decade, owning a farm that mostly runs itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd automate the washing and the feeding, about fifty thousand over two years. I'd build the direct sales up to a quarter of our pigs. By year three I'd look at buying a small neighbouring farm if the price was right, because land and robots together are where the value is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd feel like I'm steering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got one to six months saved and a barn loan. Isn't buying land a stretch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and I'd only do it with Miguel's parents as partners, keeping it in the family. If the numbers don't work in a bad year, we don't do it. I don't gamble the home farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mateo and Rosa about their futures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to fix things and learn to run a business. Mateo's already welding in the shop with his grandpa. Rosa's nine and she sells eggs at church, she's a natural.

S3.say: I'd tell every producer I know that five years is plenty for a family farm that pays attention: get your numbers straight, learn the machines and find your customers.
S3.think: We'd come out well, watching the big companies make costly mistakes first and buying second-generation kit cheaper. By the end of the decade I'd own a farm that mostly runs itself.
S3.do: Automates washing and feeding for about fifty thousand over two years and builds direct sales to a quarter of the pigs. By year three considers buying a small neighbouring farm with Miguel's parents as partners, only if the numbers work in a bad year.
S3.quote: If the numbers don't work in a bad year, we don't do it. I don't gamble the home farm.
S3.fieldNote: Five years puts Dana in her element: time to let others make mistakes and then buy in cheaper. Her risk-taking has a firm floor, keeping the home farm safe and the family as partners. Her children's skills, welding and selling eggs, show the values she wants to pass on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift. Any family farm that's not ready by then wasn't trying. I'd say it kindly, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm not worried about the farm at all. What worries me is the town. If nobody needs to work in barns or shops, what holds the church and the school together? Work gives people a reason to get up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do it all at a steady pace, one big machine every couple of years, paid off before the next. I'd put money aside for both kids' training. And I'd talk to the pastor about the church running something for people who lose work, a skills group or a farm share, so they keep busy and connected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about us. Uneasy about the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said work gives people a reason to get up. Would you still work if a robot ran the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every day. I'd find something. Breeding better pigs, selling, teaching the young families at church. I can't imagine sitting still, and I don't think God made us to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The farrowing room at night, when a litter comes right and the sow settles. That's the bit that's mine. A camera can tell me it happened, but it can't feel it for me.

S4.say: I'd say kindly but plainly that ten years is a gift, and any family farm not ready by then wasn't trying.
S4.think: I'm not worried about the farm at all, but about the town. If nobody needs to work in barns or shops, I don't know what holds the church and school together.
S4.do: Brings in one big machine every couple of years, paying each off before the next, and saves for both children's training. Asks the pastor about a church skills group or farm share for people who lose work.
S4.feel: Calm about the family, uneasy about the town.
S4.quote: A camera can tell me it happened, but it can't feel it for me.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade Dana has no fear for her own farm and turns her worry to the town and church. Her faith shapes her belief that people need work to live well. She would keep working even if robots ran everything, and named the farrowing room at night as what she'd miss.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the big companies have the cash to move first and we'd be racing them with a barn loan. What would help is banks willing to lend to family farms on fair terms, and fewer regulations slowing us down while the big boys roll ahead.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what people do with their time if the work's gone. Everyone's asking about money. I'm more worried about Saturday mornings with nothing to do.

headlineQuote: If nobody needs to work in barns or shops, what holds the church and the school together?
portrait: Dana Alvarez is 43 and runs Cedar Hill, a farrow-to-finish pig and grain farm she owns with her husband Miguel, handling the pigs and every piece of technology while he runs the crops. She uses AI every day for feed and books, believes in free markets, faith and family, and keeps Sundays screen-free. She is calm through the plateau, steady change and five- and ten-year AGI, seeing robots as good for owner-operators, and only uneasy at two years because big pork companies would outspend a family with a barn loan. Her deeper worry is not her farm but what happens to the church, the town and her children's work ethic if nobody needs to work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because big companies have the cash to move first while her family races them with a barn loan.
whatWouldHelp: Banks lending to family farms on fair terms, and fewer regulations slowing small farms while the big companies move ahead.
